title: Nietzsche
summary: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher who called for a "revaluation of all values" and for saying "yes" to life in all its fullness, pain included. He criticized a morality built on guilt and hidden resentment, and looked for ways to live more strongly, more freely and more creatively.
onEmotions: Nietzsche trusted the body and the feelings more than abstract reason: for him the affects are the forces a person is made of. He didn't call for suppressing them but advised "sublimating" them — channeling them into creation. He saw suffering not as an argument against life but as material from which one can grow. Yet he was merciless toward feelings that, in his view, poison life from within: "ressentiment" (hidden, festering resentment), self-flagellation, and pity that humiliates. His ideal is amor fati — love of one's fate as a whole.

anxiety.text: Nietzsche would ask something unexpected about your anxiety: what if it is a force that has nowhere to go yet? And he would not ask you to be ashamed of it. He himself lived his whole life with illness, insomnia and uncertainty. His key idea here is the "will to power", often crudely read as a thirst for domination. But for Nietzsche it is above all life's urge to grow and to overcome itself; it's no accident that one chapter of Zarathustra is called "On Self-Overcoming". So anxiety is a life force that senses a challenge ahead but doesn't yet know where to go. Nietzsche advised not running from the tension but turning it into movement, into creation, into one small step. Then anxiety is not an enemy but raw material from which something of your own can be born.
anxiety.practice: "The sedentary life is the real sin against the Holy Spirit," Nietzsche wrote. Take a brisk ten-minute walk and let the anxious energy run into your legs; on the way, choose one small task to channel it into.

fear.text: At twenty-six Nietzsche went to the Franco-Prussian War as a medical orderly, carried the wounded and fell ill himself with dysentery and diphtheria. He knew fear well and never thought courage meant its absence. In the fourth part of Thus Spoke Zarathustra he says that courage belongs to the one who knows fear but masters it, who sees the abyss but looks into it with pride, with the eyes of an eagle. It follows that fear is not a reason to doubt yourself but part of any real step. Nietzsche believed growth is impossible without going beyond the familiar, and so without uncertainty. If you are afraid, it may mean you are standing on the threshold of something that matters. You don't have to step forward right away. To begin, it's enough to admit: "I'm afraid, and I'm still here" — that is already a small courage.
fear.practice: Stand up straight and look out of the window the way Zarathustra's eagle looks into the abyss — calmly, from a height. Say aloud: "I'm afraid, and I'm still here."

sadness.text: "Without music, life would be a mistake," wrote Nietzsche, who composed songs and sat down at the piano almost every day. He knew sadness well and never thought it shameful. In the preface to the second edition of The Gay Science he writes that great pain is the liberator of the spirit: he doubts that it makes us "better", but he is sure it makes us deeper. Yet he did not romanticize suffering for its own sake. His goal was "the great health": the ability to pass through pain and come back with a new outlook and a new love of life. In other words, sadness is not a failure but part of how life digests experience. Nietzsche would suggest not hiding your sadness and not hurrying it, but one day asking: what is it teaching me, who am I as I come out of it? You don't need to answer that today — you can simply keep the question nearby.
sadness.practice: Put on music in which your sadness can be heard: Nietzsche believed music knows more about feelings than words do. Listen to the end and ask yourself: who am I as I come out of this melody?

grief.text: Nietzsche's father, a village pastor, died when the boy was four, and his son remembered all his life how he had improvised at the piano. Grief is one of the hardest things to live through, and it needs time. Soon afterward his younger brother died too. His idea of amor fati — love of one's fate — sounds especially hard in grief, and it is easy to misunderstand. It is not about rejoicing in a loss or pretending it doesn't hurt. It is more about coming, in time, to accept your life as a whole — including the people you loved and what bound you together. Think this through, and saying "yes" to life means saying "yes" to this love, too, the love that hurts right now. Such a "yes" isn't spoken in a day; it is a long road on which grief remains part of a love story.
grief.practice: Say quietly, "I am grateful that my life held…" — and name the person. Let the pain stay beside that sentence: the two don't need to argue.

loneliness.text: In summer Nietzsche lived in Sils-Maria, in a small rented room, and walked alone for hours along the Alpine lakes; in winter, in strangers' boarding houses in Genoa and Nice. He knew loneliness as few have, and if you are painfully lonely now, he would understand. But he learned to tell loneliness as abandonment apart from solitude as a space where a person can hear themselves, far from the "flies of the marketplace" — the bustle and noise Zarathustra speaks of. Then loneliness can be not only a deprivation but also a time when you become yourself rather than who others want you to be. And yet Nietzsche longed deeply for friendship — for people who would share not pity but joy and growth. You might gently ask yourself: what part of this time alone can I make my own, and what kind of closeness is worth tending to?
loneliness.practice: Sit in silence for five minutes, like Nietzsche by an Alpine lake — no phone, no background noise. Listen for the wish or thought that sounds in you only when no one is around.

anger.text: Nietzsche called himself "dynamite" and philosophized, as he put it, with a hammer. For him anger was a living force, not a disgrace: open, honest anger, he thought, can be healthier than a polite smile. Far more dangerous, in his view, was "ressentiment" — a hidden grudge that isn't expressed but builds up and turns into quiet revenge, into a wish to see the offender humiliated. In On the Genealogy of Morals he describes how the powerlessness to respond turns into long bitterness. This means what matters is not suppressing anger but recognizing it: is this a direct energy that wants to protect what is yours, or an old grudge poisoning you from within? Nietzsche admired those who can quickly "shake off" offences — not out of weakness but out of an abundance of strength, so as to go on living.
anger.practice: Let the anger out through movement: walk briskly or loosen your shoulders and fists, as if before a fight that won't happen. Then ask yourself: is this about what's happening now, or about an old grudge?

shame.text: A pastor's son raised among pious aunts, Nietzsche learned early how heavy another's stern gaze can be. If you are painfully ashamed right now, this is not your fault. Nietzsche saw sharply how society uses shame to make people obedient. In On the Genealogy of Morals he showed how morality can turn a person against themselves — make them ashamed of their own strengths, desires, body. And in The Gay Science there is a short series of questions and answers: whom do you call bad? The one who always wants to put others to shame. What is most humane to you? To spare someone shame. In Nietzsche's terms, shame is often someone else's voice that has settled inside you. Nietzsche proposed gradually reclaiming the right to be yourself, and treating yourself as tenderly as a friend you want to spare from shame.
shame.practice: Imagine a close friend is feeling your shame. What would you say to spare them from it — the most humane thing, for Nietzsche? Now say it aloud to yourself.

quote.text: What is the seal of liberation? — No longer being ashamed in front of oneself.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

guilt.text: Nietzsche wrote On the Genealogy of Morals like an investigation: where, exactly, did this feeling in us — "I am guilty" — come from? If guilt weighs on you now, he would suggest not only carrying it but taking a closer look at it. In the second essay of On the Genealogy of Morals he noticed that the German word Schuld means both "guilt" and "debt": in his view, the feeling of guilt grew out of the relationship between debtor and creditor. And he described "bad conscience" as a force that found no outlet and turned back against the person themselves. Seen this way, not all guilt is the voice of truth: part of it is a habit of punishing yourself. Nietzsche valued the person who can stand behind their promises, but he opposed self-torment. Following him, you can draw a distinction: responsibility looks forward — what can I do? — while self-flagellation goes around in circles.
guilt.practice: Tap your guilt with Nietzsche's "hammer," as if it were an idol: ask it, "What can I fix?" — and listen for whether the answer rings true. If it does, take that step; if it sounds hollow, it is most likely a habit of punishing yourself.

envy.text: The Olympic games, contests of poets, arguments of philosophers — the Greeks, as Nietzsche observed, lived by rivalry and were not ashamed of it. Envy is a very human feeling, and Nietzsche himself didn't pretend to be free of it. In his early essay "Homer's Contest" he recalls that the ancient Greeks, following Hesiod, distinguished two goddesses of strife, two Erises: an evil one that leads to hostility, and a good one that stirs the jealous desire to match another and surpass them in deeds. In this light, envy can be not only destructive but also a call to your own growth. Nietzsche warned of the danger when it turns into "ressentiment" — the wish to belittle another so as not to have to grow yourself. A good question, then: what is this envy calling me toward — not to take from someone else, but to create something of my own?
envy.practice: Call on the good Eris: name exactly what stung you in someone else, and take one small step today toward your own version of it — not taking from them, but creating something of your own.

emptiness.text: "God is dead" — in Nietzsche these words are spoken by a madman who runs through the marketplace in broad daylight with a lantern. Emptiness and apathy can be very heavy, and you can acknowledge them without reproaching yourself. Nietzsche gave a name to a similar state of a whole era: "nihilism" — when the highest values "devalue themselves" and it seems that nothing has meaning. He saw this not as a personal weakness but as a shared experience of modern people whose old foundations had collapsed (his famous formula "God is dead" speaks precisely of this collapse). But for him nihilism was not an end point but a transition: emptiness makes room for values a person creates for themselves. So emptiness can be a beginning rather than an end. You don't need to find a grand purpose at once: sometimes a small "why" is enough — for whom or for what you'd like to live through today.
emptiness.practice: Nietzsche liked to say that whoever has a "why" can bear almost any "how." Find the smallest "why" for today — a cup of coffee, a call, a walk — and do it for its sake.

quote.text: If we have our own why of life, we shall get along with almost any how.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
quote.source: Twilight of the Idols, "Maxims and Arrows", 12 (1889)

confusion.text: "One must still have chaos in oneself to give birth to a dancing star," says Zarathustra. When the old landmarks no longer work and new ones haven't appeared, it can be frightening. Nietzsche saw a creative possibility in this state. These words come from the prologue to Zarathustra. It follows that chaos inside is not a sign that you are lost forever but material from which something new can take shape. Nietzsche also spoke of "perspectivism": there is no single correct view of the world, only many perspectives. Confusion often grows stronger when we look for the "one right" answer. You can ease that pressure: look at the situation from several sides and allow yourself not to know for a while.
confusion.practice: Look at the situation literally from three places: stand by the window, by the door, sit on the floor — and from each spot tell yourself how it looks from here. Nietzsche would call it perspectivism.

quote.text: I say unto you: one must still have chaos in oneself to be able to give birth to a dancing star.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

fatigue.text: Nietzsche rose at dawn, washed in cold water and went off into the mountains for hours — that was how he rested and how he thought. Tiredness and burnout are not laziness but a sign that more strength has been spent than restored. Nietzsche, who suffered from illness all his life, paid very close attention to the body. In the chapter "On the Despisers of the Body", Zarathustra calls the body a "great reason", and what we call the mind merely its "little reason". In other words, tiredness is a reasonable message from the body, not an obstacle. In The Gay Science Nietzsche also noted that modern people are ashamed of rest and rush about as if afraid of being left alone with themselves. For him, walks, sunshine, good air and quiet were a serious part of thinking, not a waste of time. Rest, for Nietzsche, is not weakness but a condition of strength.
fatigue.practice: Ask your body — your "great reason," as Nietzsche called it — what it needs right now. Grant its smallest request: lie down, drink something, step outside.

boredom.text: Sailors feared a dead calm more than a storm — and Nietzsche, who lived in the port city of Genoa, borrowed this image for boredom. Boredom is unpleasant, and we often want to escape it into entertainment as fast as possible. Nietzsche offered an unexpected view. In The Gay Science he writes that for thinkers and sensitive people boredom is that disagreeable "windless calm of the soul" that precedes a happy voyage and cheerful winds. He noticed that whoever fears boredom too much is forced to chase endlessly after activity for its own sake. Think this through, and boredom is not wasted time but a pause in which something of your own ripens. Nietzsche advised enduring it rather than drowning it out. Perhaps your boredom is exactly that calm after which the wind will rise.
boredom.practice: Spend five minutes in the "calm": sit down, switch nothing on, and don't drown the boredom out with anything. Notice which wind — a thought, a wish — rises first.

joy.text: "I would believe only in a god who knew how to dance," says Zarathustra. Nietzsche would be glad if you gave yourself to your joy completely. He named one of his books The Gay Science and believed that joy is not frivolity but the highest expression of life. His famous idea of "eternal recurrence" works as a test: would you want to live this moment again and again, endlessly? If the joy is real, the answer is yes. Then joy is the moment when you say a full "yes" to life. It needs no justification, and you needn't be ashamed of it in the face of others' troubles. Nietzsche believed that the ability to rejoice is a strength worth protecting and cultivating, not a luxury.
joy.practice: Dance — even for half a minute, even with just your shoulders, to any music or none: Nietzsche thought dancing the best answer to joy. Then ask yourself whether you'd want to live this moment again.

quote.text: All joy wants eternity — wants deep, wants deep eternity.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

love.text: At Tribschen, Wagner's villa on Lake Lucerne, the young Nietzsche spent what he later called the happiest days of his life. Love and tenderness are of enormous value, and for all his sharpness he wrote about them deeply. He distinguished love that makes the other stronger from love that keeps them weak. He was critical of "compassion" in the sense of pity: he believed pity can humiliate the one who is pitied and multiply suffering. But he greatly valued "shared joy" — the ability to rejoice together with another; in Human, All Too Human he writes that what makes a friend is not shared suffering but shared joy. This means tenderness is especially precious when it believes in the other's strength. Zarathustra also speaks of "love of the farthest" — of who a person may become. To love is to see someone's future in them.
love.practice: Today, tell someone close to you what you are sincerely glad about for them — this is Nietzsche's "shared joy." Notice how the conversation changes.

gratitude.text: On 15 October 1888, his forty-fourth birthday, Nietzsche sat down to write Ecce Homo. The warm feeling of gratitude was almost sacred to him. He opens his autobiographical book Ecce Homo with words about a "perfect day" on which he asks himself: how could I fail to be grateful to my whole life? This was written by a man who had lived through serious illness, loneliness and lack of recognition. In Nietzsche's terms, gratitude for Nietzsche is not politeness for strokes of luck but gratitude to life as a whole, with all its difficulties — close to amor fati. Yet he would be against gratitude under compulsion: it should be free, born of abundance. It doesn't need to be forced; you can simply notice where it arises on its own.
gratitude.practice: Read Nietzsche's line aloud: "How could I fail to be grateful to my whole life?" — and name one hard thing in your past from which something valuable grew over time. If there's no gratitude yet, simply notice that.

hope.text: Half-blind and worn down by migraines, Nietzsche moved to the sea every winter, hoping the sun would give him back his strength. Hope sustains us, and holding on to it is natural. Nietzsche had a complicated relationship with hope. In Human, All Too Human he offers a provocative reading of the Pandora myth: hope stayed in the box as the most treacherous of evils, because it only prolongs torment. This can be read not as a call to give up but as a warning against passively waiting for things to change on their own. Nietzsche set creative will against that kind of hope: not only to wait for a better future but to take part in making it. And the same Nietzsche, through Zarathustra, urges us to hold our highest hope sacred. Seen this way, the most Nietzschean hope is the one that turns into action, however small.
hope.practice: Turn one hope into an action for this week — the smallest one: set a date, ask, begin. Nietzsche would say that this is how hope stops being waiting and becomes will.

quote.text: But by my love and hope I beseech you: do not throw away the hero in your soul! Hold holy your highest hope!
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
quote.source: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, "On the Tree on the Mountainside" (1883)

nostalgia.text: At fourteen Nietzsche had already written his first autobiography — that's how early he began looking back on the past. Nostalgia is a tender longing for what has passed, and there is a great deal of love in it. Nietzsche offered an unusual view of the past. His idea of "eternal recurrence" (first in The Gay Science, § 341) goes like this: imagine that you will have to live your life once more and innumerable times more, with all its joys and hardships. For him this was a way to test whether you can say "yes" to your life. In this light, nostalgia is already a partial "yes": you love what was so much that you would like to go back. Nietzsche proposed widening this "yes": not only to long for the best parts but to accept the whole road that brought you here. That is amor fati — love of fate.
nostalgia.practice: Imagine that you have to walk the whole road again, from the time you miss to today. What of that road are you ready to accept — even if not all of it at once?

quote.text: My formula for greatness in a human being is amor fati: that one wants nothing to be different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
quote.source: Ecce Homo, "Why I Am So Clever", 10

craving.text: Who in you is saying "I want it now" — and who else is in there? Nietzsche saw a person as many forces, not one voice. A sharp craving says nothing bad about you. Nietzsche took the drives seriously and without moralizing. In Daybreak (§ 109) he lists ways a person can deal with the vehemence of a drive: avoiding occasions for it, bringing regularity into one's life, diverting one's energies to other work, linking the desire to a clear thought of its consequences. And he adds a sober remark: even the wish to fight a drive is itself a drive, another force within us. So a craving is not all of you but only one voice among many. There are other forces in you — the one that wants clarity, health, freedom. You can call on them for help without scolding yourself.
craving.practice: Name one more force in you besides the craving — for example, the wish for a clear morning. Give it one small action right now: step outside, drink some water, call someone.

addiction.text: How do you take back the master's place in your own life? Nietzsche called this path self-overcoming and knew it is never quick. Addiction is a long-standing circle that is hard to leave, and it is not a moral failure. Nietzsche, who lived his whole life with pain and illness, thought a great deal about how a suffering person seeks relief from pain. In the Genealogy of Morals he described the urge to deaden pain with a strong emotion as something deeply human, but he also saw a trap in it: such relief only numbs the suffering without touching its cause. And in The Gay Science (§ 295) he confesses that he loves "brief habits" that come and go, but is weighed down by habits that hold a person for years. It follows that addiction is a means that has become the master. Nietzsche would wish for you to take back the place of master — not through shame, but through gradual "self-overcoming".
addiction.practice: Tell someone you trust, "This habit once helped me cope with…" — and finish the sentence. If you like, you can start the same conversation with people who have walked a similar road — for example, in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: What do you do with yesterday's self when your body aches today and anxiety, shame and gaps in memory pile on top? Nietzsche would answer: to begin with, don't beat yourself up. Nietzsche, incidentally, gave up alcohol himself: in Ecce Homo he writes that even a small amount of wine or beer made his life a "vale of misery", and the best thing he found for himself was water and a clear head. But his main point here is about remorse. In Twilight of the Idols he remarks that one should not cravenly abandon one's deeds after the fact. This is not a justification of last night but an invitation not to hide from it. In other words, shame is useful if it leads to a conclusion, but harmful if it turns into self-flagellation. What conclusion do you want to take from this morning?
hangover.practice: Drink some water and open a window, the way Nietzsche threw his windows open to the mountain air. Then say aloud one lesson you want to take from last night — and don't return to the verdict.

euphoria.text: The sun, for Nietzsche, shines not because it lacks something but because it has too much light. A burst of euphoria is a vivid experience, and you can enjoy it. Nietzsche valued the fullness of life, but he drew an important distinction. In The Gay Science (§ 370) he asks: does an upsurge arise from an abundance of strength or from a lack of it? Some seek fullness because they overflow with it; others seek oblivion, numbing, to get away from themselves for a while. Nietzsche trusted the first and was wary of the second. Think this through, and it's worth simply noticing: where did this wave come from? If from an encounter, a discovery, beauty — stay in it; this is what Nietzsche called "the great health". If it feels more like an escape, that is no reason for reproach either, just a piece of information about yourself.
euphoria.practice: Ask yourself aloud: "Does this joy come from fullness, or from a wish to get away from something?" Hear the first answer without judging it, and give yourself a minute simply to stand in the light.

crash.text: Can you fall from a height and not take it as a verdict? Nietzsche tested this on himself many times. A sharp drop after a high can be very hard. Nietzsche knew such swings well: for him, bursts of creative energy alternated with weeks of illness. In the third part of Thus Spoke Zarathustra there is a chapter called "The Convalescent": after enormous strain Zarathustra collapses and lies for seven days without strength, while his animals take care of him. When he rises, they tell him the world is waiting for him like a garden. Then a crash is not a refutation of the high but its other side, a time when strength is restored. Nietzsche wouldn't urge you to get up immediately. He would remind you that convalescence is also part of the road, and that afterward the world can become a garden again.
crash.practice: Look after yourself the way the animals looked after Zarathustra for seven days: warm food, a blanket, fresh air — choose one. Notice how your body responds.

panic.text: Nietzsche, whose attacks of illness sometimes lasted for days, would never tell you to "pull yourself together": your heart pounds, your breath falters, your thoughts race toward the worst, and it is genuinely hard. Nietzsche trusted the body more than many philosophers did: he wrote that behind our thoughts and feelings stands the body, and that it is wiser than it seems. In the Prologue to Zarathustra there is a call: "remain faithful to the earth." This means in panic your thoughts fly off into terrifying pictures, while your body and the earth stay here, beneath you. A wave like this usually rises, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Nietzsche would suggest not arguing with the wave in your head, but literally feeling the ground — the support that is holding you right now.
panic.practice: Press your feet into the floor and say to yourself, "Faithful to the earth." Feel it holding you, breathe out longer than you breathe in, and name five things you can see.

dread.text: "If you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss also gazes into you" — one of Nietzsche's best-known lines. The sense of an abyss, "what's the point of it all," is one of the heaviest experiences, and Nietzsche knew it as few have. He described "nihilism": the situation in which old foundations collapse and it seems that nothing has meaning. But Nietzsche saw nihilism not as an end but as a transitional state, after which a person can create their own values. His answer is amor fati, love of one's life as a whole. At the same time he warned against gazing too long into the abyss. In Nietzsche's terms, your dread is not the discovery of "the truth" but an honest encounter with a big question. You don't have to answer it right away: sometimes it is enough to turn your gaze from the abyss to what holds you here — people, tasks, the day.
dread.practice: Turn your gaze from the abyss literally: look out of the window at something alive and near — a tree, people, the light. Name three things holding you today, and stay with each for a few seconds.

quote.text: And if you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss also gazes into you.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

fomo.text: Nietzsche lived in small rooms, with almost no money and no audience — and there he wrote books the whole world now reads. The feeling that everyone else lives more interesting lives and you're not where you should be is exhausting. Nietzsche would describe it as the power of the "herd" — the habit of measuring yourself by what everyone does. In his essay "Schopenhauer as Educator" he writes that every person is unique and exists only once, yet most hide behind common opinions and habits. Conscience, he says, calls out: "Be yourself." Seen this way, the fear of missing out is a fear of missing someone else's life, not your own. Nietzsche would propose the test of "eternal recurrence": not "what is everyone doing?" but "which day of my own would I want to live again and again?" The answer almost never matches someone else's feed.
fomo.practice: Run the thought experiment of eternal recurrence: which ordinary day of your own would you want to live again and again — not for an audience, but for yourself? Do one thing from that day today.

sleepless.text: For many years Nietzsche was tormented by insomnia and knew how huge and unsolvable thoughts seem at three in the morning. Nietzsche knew this firsthand — insomnia tormented him for many years. In Zarathustra there is a chapter, "On the Teachers of Virtue", where a sage teaches good sleep: during the day you must overcome yourself ten times, reconcile ten times, laugh ten times — and then sleep will come at night. Zarathustra laughs at this "sage", but the picture itself is touching: sleep depends more on the day you've lived than on fighting insomnia at night. In this light, right now you don't need to force yourself to sleep or settle every question. Night is not the time for verdicts. You can simply lie there and rest, even without sleep.
sleepless.practice: Recall one moment from today when you smiled or made peace with something — as the "sage" in Zarathustra advises. Hold it in your memory as you breathe out slowly.

betrayal.text: How do you go on when the one you trusted most turns out to be someone else? Nietzsche had to answer this question in his early thirties. Betrayal destroys not only a relationship but your trust in your own judgment. Nietzsche knew this from experience: his friendship with Wagner, which he had once treasured above all else, ended in a bitter break. In The Gay Science there is a passage called "Star Friendship": we were friends and have become strangers, we are like two ships, each with its own course — and yet what was remains. So betrayal doesn't cancel the good you lived through, and doesn't make you naive for having trusted. Nietzsche warned of something else, too: not to let the hurt turn into "ressentiment", which poisons from within. Your pain is legitimate, but you are bigger than this wound.
betrayal.practice: Slowly read the opening of Nietzsche's "Star Friendship": "We were friends and have become estranged." Name one thing from this relationship you want to keep, despite how it all ended.

quote.text: We were friends and have become estranged.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

jealousy.text: In 1882 Nietzsche, his friend Paul Rée and Lou Salomé dreamed of living together as a "holy trinity" of friendship and thought — and jealousy destroyed the alliance. Burning jealousy is nothing to be ashamed of: it shows how much a person means to you. Nietzsche looked at it without illusions. In The Gay Science (§ 14) he wrote that love between people often turns out to be a lust for possession: the lover wants to possess the other exclusively. But he also described another possibility: when two people's desire to possess each other gives way to a shared longing for something higher than both of them. He called that kind of love friendship. It follows that jealousy is love that is still holding on rather than looking in the same direction. Nietzsche wouldn't shame you for it; he would suggest asking: what could this person and I love together?
jealousy.practice: Name one thing you and this person love together — a book, a place, a cause. Picture the two of you looking at it side by side rather than at each other, and notice what changes.

resentment.text: "Consider the herd grazing past you": the cows don't remember yesterday — this is how Nietzsche opens his essay on the uses and disadvantages of history, almost envying their forgetfulness. An old grudge is a heavy burden, and there is almost always real pain behind it. Nietzsche devoted an entire study, On the Genealogy of Morals, to this feeling, which he called by the French word "ressentiment". Ressentiment, in his view, is pain that found no outlet and is chewed over inside again and again. Nietzsche said there is no strength in it, only poisoning. He saw the way out in "active forgetfulness" — not in forgiving under duress, but in "digesting" what happened, the way a healthy stomach digests food. In Ecce Homo he admits that freedom from ressentiment was one of the main lessons his illness taught him. In other words, letting go of a grudge is worth doing not for the sake of the one who hurt you but for the sake of your own life.
resentment.practice: Go for a walk and try to "digest" the grudge, as Nietzsche advised: with every tenth step, let go of one thought about it. When you come back, ask yourself what a little space has been freed up for.

heartbreak.text: In the winter of 1883, in Rapallo, Nietzsche wrote the first part of Zarathustra in ten days — only months after the hardest break of his life. A broken heart is one of the sharpest pains, and it shouldn't be hurried. Nietzsche went through it himself: in 1882 his attachment to Lou Salomé came to an end, and with it a friendship on which he had placed great hopes. The break wounded him deeply. Think this through, and great pain is not only destruction: for Nietzsche it became the source of one of his central works. He said that great pain makes a person deeper. You don't need to turn your grief into an achievement right now. But perhaps one day you'll see that you came out of it carrying something new.
heartbreak.practice: Walk, as Nietzsche did along the roads above Rapallo, and let the pain walk beside you without chasing it away. On the way back, name one thing this love revealed to you about yourself.

impostor.text: At twenty-four Nietzsche became a professor at Basel before he had even defended a dissertation — perfect soil for the feeling that you're about to be found out. That feeling especially often visits people who are demanding of themselves. Nietzsche helps you look at it differently. In Zarathustra he writes that the human being is a bridge, not a goal: we are always on the way, in the process of becoming. The subtitle of his autobiography Ecce Homo is "How One Becomes What One Is": not what one is, but how one becomes. Then the feeling "I'm not yet who I'm supposed to be" is not the exposure of a fraud but the ordinary state of a growing person. The inner "impostor" expects you to be finished already. Nietzsche would say: no one is ever finished. You are in your place precisely because you keep growing.
impostor.practice: Tell yourself aloud: "A human being is a bridge, not a goal. I'm still learning…" — and name one thing in which you are growing right now. Allow yourself to be on the way, not at the finish.

self_hatred.text: "One must learn to love oneself with a wholesome and healthy love, so that one can bear to be with oneself and need not roam," says Zarathustra. A harsh inner critic causes enormous pain, and you do not deserve that verdict. Nietzsche showed where such a voice can come from. In On the Genealogy of Morals he described "bad conscience" as a force that found no outlet and turned back against the person themselves. Self-flagellation, in his view, doesn't make us better — it only poisons life. That is why he was so merciless toward a morality that teaches self-contempt. This means the inner critic is not the voice of truth but a learned habit. And in Zarathustra Nietzsche offers a different teaching: to love yourself with a healthy love. Not to admire yourself blindly, but to learn to bear yourself and be your own ally.
self_hatred.practice: Say aloud one sentence from your inner critic, and then the answer a loyal friend would give you. Repeat the second one again, more slowly.

quote.text: One must learn to love oneself — thus I teach — with a wholesome and healthy love, so that one can bear to be with oneself and need not roam.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
quote.source: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, "On the Spirit of Gravity", 2 (1884)

helplessness.text: Amor fati — love of fate — was coined by a man who for years could barely read because of the pain in his eyes. Feeling that you can't change anything is very heavy, and it is not your fault. Nietzsche knew powerlessness firsthand: for years illness kept him from working, reading, leaving his room. In Ecce Homo he writes that in such periods he learned to conserve his strength: not to fight everything at once, but to accept his situation as given. From this experience grew his idea of amor fati, love of fate. It is not resignation but a calm "yes" to what already is, from which the next step can grow. In Nietzsche's terms, even in powerlessness one space of freedom remains — your attitude toward what is happening. Sometimes that is exactly where change begins.
helplessness.practice: Tell yourself, "This is how it is right now," and take three slow out-breaths. Then choose one tiny thing you can do for yourself within the limits of what is — and do it.

procrastination.text: Whoever wants to learn to fly one day, Nietzsche teaches, must first learn to stand, walk, run, climb and dance — one cannot fly into flying. The "I can't get started" state is draining, and it doesn't mean you're lazy. Nietzsche would call it "the spirit of gravity" — the name Zarathustra gives to the force that drags you down and makes everything heavy and serious. Zarathustra sets lightness, laughter and dance against it. Seen this way, procrastination is often born not of unwillingness but of the task having grown too heavy in your imagination. Nietzsche also knew a simple remedy: in Twilight of the Idols he writes that only thoughts reached by walking have any value. He himself thought on the move — for many hours a day. Sometimes what helps you start is not willpower but moving your body and a little more lightness.
procrastination.practice: Walk for a few minutes, thinking about the task but not solving it: Nietzsche trusted only thoughts that came while walking. When you come back, take only the very first, easiest step.

uprooted.text: For twenty years Nietzsche moved between Basel, Sils-Maria, Genoa, Nice and Turin, and his luggage was often a trunk of books and manuscripts. Being torn from home is a hard experience, and homesickness is legitimate. Nietzsche knew this state deeply: in 1869 he gave up his Prussian citizenship and lived the rest of his life stateless, wandering between Switzerland, Italy and the south of France. One of his books is called The Wanderer and His Shadow, and in The Gay Science there is a passage titled "We Who Are Homeless". In this light, losing a home is not only a loss but also a chance to see the world with fresh eyes, without belonging to it entirely. Nietzsche didn't deny the pain of wandering. But he learned to carry home within himself: in his thoughts, his walks, his work.
uprooted.practice: Perform your own portable ritual today — like Nietzsche's daily walk in whatever city he was in: one habit you can take anywhere, such as morning tea, a short walk, a favourite tune.

overload.text: Nietzsche was one of the first philosophers to write on a typewriter, and he noticed that our writing tools are also working on our thoughts. Overload, the endless feed and information noise really are tiring, and you don't have to keep up with everything. Nietzsche described a similar problem almost a century and a half ago. In Twilight of the Idols he says that the first thing to learn is "to see": to accustom the eye to calm and patience, to let things come to you rather than reacting instantly to every stimulus. He considered the inability not to respond to a stimulus a sign of exhaustion, not of strength. So overload is when every stimulus yanks us around. Nietzsche would suggest not even more effort but a pause: learning not to grab at everything at once — to decline, to postpone, to choose.
overload.practice: Practise seeing, as Nietzsche advised: pick one object in front of you and look at it for a minute without getting distracted. Notice how your attention changes.

unreality.text: What if the "real world" isn't somewhere behind the scenes but right here, under your feet? Nietzsche came to this conclusion over many years. When everything around you feels unreal, it's frightening, and it can be hard to talk about. In Twilight of the Idols there is a short text, "How the 'True World' Finally Became a Fable": it shows how for centuries philosophers considered some other world to be the real one, and this one mere appearance. Nietzsche's conclusion is unexpected: if we abolish the "true world", this world stops being "apparent" — it is the only one, and it is real. It follows that even when everything feels distant, this world — your body, the ground, the things around you — is reality. The feeling will pass, and the ground will stay under your feet.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a distinct texture — fabric, wood, cold water. Say aloud, "This is here, and I am here" — Nietzsche would call it faithfulness to the earth.

awe.text: Nietzsche called the mountain air of the Engadine his best medicine and said the landscape there was kin to him. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience. In Ecce Homo he recalls how in the summer of 1881, walking by Lake Silvaplana in the Alps, he stopped by a huge pyramid-shaped rock — and there the thought of "eternal recurrence" came to him, which he wrote down with the note "6,000 feet beyond man and time". Music was another source of awe for him. In other words, awe is a moment when life shows its depth and you want to say a full "yes" to it. You don't need to do anything with this feeling. Just let it be.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with whatever filled you with awe, and ask yourself the question of eternal recurrence: would I want to live this again — and once more?

quote.text: Without music, life would be an error.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
quote.source: Twilight of the Idols, "Maxims and Arrows", 33 (1889)

relief.text: What does life taste like when the weight finally lifts? Nietzsche knew the answer from his many recoveries. Relief is a warm feeling after a long heaviness, and it is worth savoring. Nietzsche described it in the preface to the second edition of The Gay Science. He says the book was written in a state of convalescence: it is the joy of a spirit that has long endured a burden and now breathes again. There he also notes that after a long illness a person returns to life with a new taste, more sensitive to joy. Think this through, and relief is not just the end of something hard but the beginning of a new capacity for joy. Nietzsche wouldn't rush you toward new achievements. He would suggest simply savoring this taste — the taste of someone who has come back.
relief.practice: Eat or drink something simple — an apple, some tea — slowly, like the convalescent Nietzsche wrote about. Notice how much brighter the taste has become.

calm.text: What is left of a stormy philosopher when he lies down under a tree at noon? Calm is a precious state in which it's good simply to be, and Nietzsche gave it one of his quietest chapters. This is the chapter "At Noon" in the fourth part of Zarathustra. Zarathustra lies down under a tree in the midday stillness, and it seems to him that the world has just become perfect. He says that very little is needed for happiness: the rustle of a lizard, a breath of air, a moment. The least thing, he writes, makes the best happiness. Then your calm is not a pause between tasks but one of life's peaks. Nietzsche wouldn't analyze it. He would only suggest listening more quietly to this noon.
calm.practice: Sit in silence and find one very small thing around you — a sound, a breath of air, the light. Stay with it for a minute, like Zarathustra under the tree at noon.

inspiration.text: "A thought flashes up like lightning, with necessity, without hesitation — I never had any choice," Nietzsche recalled of writing Zarathustra. If inspiration has seized you now, it is worth embracing fully. Nietzsche described it with extraordinary vividness. Such thoughts, he said, came with a feeling of strength and freedom. He admits that many thoughts came to him on long walks. This means inspiration is a moment when something larger than your everyday "I" is at work in you. Nietzsche wouldn't analyze it. He would say: accept this gift and write it down while it's here, and then, as he did, take a walk and let it continue.
inspiration.practice: Write down what came to you without editing it — like Nietzsche, who jotted thoughts in a notebook as he walked. Then go for a short walk and notice what gets added.

schadenfreude.text: Why does someone else's failure suddenly bring relief? Nietzsche looked for the answer without moralizing. Admitting schadenfreude to yourself is awkward, but almost everyone knows it. Nietzsche didn't pretend this feeling was rare, and he looked for its roots. In The Wanderer and His Shadow he explained it this way: a person who is doing badly sees another's misfortune and feels they are "equals" again — this soothes their envy. In the Genealogy of Morals he described a deeper mechanism, too — "ressentiment", the hidden grudge of powerlessness that seeks comfort in the humiliation of others. In Nietzsche's terms, schadenfreude is not a verdict on your character but a signal: somewhere you feel hurt or left behind. Nietzsche saw the way out not in self-flagellation but in taking this energy back for yourself: not waiting for others to fall, but building your own rise.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself where you feel left behind right now — and take one small step today toward your own rise. Nietzsche would say: don't wait for others to fall; build your own.

contempt.text: "I love the great despisers, because they are the great reverers," says Zarathustra. Contempt is a cold feeling, and there can be both rightness and pain in it. Nietzsche's attitude to it was ambivalent, and that is what makes him interesting. Only someone who longs with all their heart for something else, he thought, can despise something strongly. Seen this way, your contempt may point to what you truly value. But in the Genealogy of Morals Nietzsche distinguished two kinds of disdain: a light one that forgets quickly, and a venomous one that chews over another's worthlessness in order to feel superior — and that is already ressentiment. A good question: does my contempt free me, or tie me to this person? What do I actually believe in, if I see so sharply that this isn't it?
contempt.practice: Finish aloud: "I despise this because I believe in…". Look at the second half — that is your value, and it deserves more of your thought than what you despise.

disgust.text: Nietzsche admitted that his greatest danger was not fear but disgust with human beings. Disgust — with people, with a situation or with yourself — can wash over you so strongly that you want to wall yourself off from everything. Nietzsche knew this feeling firsthand and made it part of his central book. His Zarathustra feels a "great disgust" with humankind, with its pettiness and sameness. In the chapter "The Convalescent" it knocks him off his feet: for seven days he lies unable to rise, while his animals look after him. What matters is how it ends: Zarathustra recovers and says "yes" to life again. In this light, disgust is not the final truth about the world or about you, but a hard stage you can pass through. Nietzsche didn't shame anyone for it. He showed that even his strongest hero fell ill with it — and that recovery lies beyond it.
disgust.practice: Open a window or step outside: Nietzsche escaped disgust in the mountain wind. Take a few deep out-breaths and find one thing to which you can say at least a quiet "yes."

revenge.text: "That man be redeemed from revenge — that is for me the bridge to the highest hope," says Zarathustra. The desire for revenge usually means you've been caused real pain, and Nietzsche didn't deny the strength of this feeling. But he considered revenge one of the deepest poisons of the human soul. In Thus Spoke Zarathustra he calls "the spirit of revenge" what keeps a person chained to the past. In the Genealogy of Morals he described how unavenged pain turns into ressentiment — a hidden grudge that poisons the one who carries it. Hence an unexpected conclusion: freedom from revenge is not weakness but the highest form of strength. Nietzsche saw it in "active forgetfulness" and in the ability not to let the one who hurt you define your life. Acknowledging your anger is honest. Refusing to hand your life over to it is the very freedom Zarathustra called for.
revenge.practice: Give yourself five minutes of "active forgetfulness," as Nietzsche called it: do something that absorbs you completely — movement, music, work with your hands. Then notice how much room in you has been freed from the one who hurt you.

quote.text: For that man be delivered from revenge, that is for me the bridge to the highest hope, and a rainbow after long storms.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

anger_at_loved.text: "In one's friend one should have one's best enemy," Nietzsche wrote, and this is true not only of friends. Anger at the people close to you is painful precisely because shame follows it. Nietzsche helps you understand both feelings. In the Genealogy of Morals he described "bad conscience": a force that finds no outlet turns inward and begins to torment the person themselves. If anger is swallowed for years, it doesn't disappear — it becomes either a sudden outburst or self-flagellation. Real closeness, for Nietzsche, can withstand disagreement. It follows that anger at someone close is not a denial of love but part of a living relationship. But Nietzsche valued strength that is master of itself. Anger deserves an honest word in a calm moment — not a blow, not a shout, and not long torture by your own shame.
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger settles, tell your loved one in one calm sentence what exactly hurt you — as an honest opponent, not a judge. Nietzsche believed such a word protects love better than silence.

ambivalence.text: Nietzsche described a human being as "a social structure of many souls," in which each drive has its own voice. Loving someone and at the same time not being able to stand them feels wrong: shouldn't a feeling be just one thing? Nietzsche thought otherwise. For him a person is not a single "I" but a multitude of drives. And in the Genealogy of Morals he formulated the principle of perspectivism: the more different affects we allow to speak about a thing, the more complete our understanding of it. In other words, your mixed feelings toward someone close are not confusion but several views of one living person. Love sees one thing, irritation another, and both can see. You don't need to pick a winner. You can listen to each feeling and see the person more fully than either would allow alone.
ambivalence.practice: Give each feeling a voice, aloud: "The love in me says…", "The irritation in me says…". What does each one see that the other doesn't?

guilty_relief.text: Who decides which feelings are "right" beside a loss? Nietzsche suspected that most often it is someone else's morality, not your heart. Relief after a breakup, a departure or the death of a seriously ill loved one often frightens us. Nietzsche was one of the most consistent critics of a morality that prescribes which feelings are "right" and makes you ashamed of the rest. He trusted the body, which he called the "great reason": it knows how long you were under strain, and it exhales when the weight lifts. Think this through, and relief is the body's honest response, not a betrayal. Nietzsche also warned about "bad conscience" — the habit of turning against yourself everything that doesn't fit the image of a good person. Relief and love can live together. You can grieve, remember, be grateful — and still feel that at last you can breathe.
guilty_relief.practice: Put a hand on your belly, breathe out slowly and tell yourself, "My 'great reason' knows how hard it was." Let the relief simply be.

indifference.text: Nietzsche, often accused of heartlessness, was, by the accounts of those who knew him, remarkably gentle and courteous in everyday life. When something "should" move you but inside it's quiet, it's easy to start reproaching yourself. Nietzsche, oddly enough, helps lift that reproach. He was suspicious of the demand to feel compassion for everything, always. In The Gay Science he wrote that a soul open to every stranger's misfortune risks losing its own path, and he advised helping first of all those whose pain you truly understand — those close to you, your friends. Then indifference to something distant or "obligatory" is not always coldness. Sometimes it is protection, sometimes honesty: you are not faking a feeling you don't have. Nietzsche valued honesty with yourself above a show of sensitivity. The only thing that matters is to ask: what actually moves me right now? That is where life is.
indifference.practice: Instead of asking "why doesn't this move me?", ask: "What actually moved me today?" Recall it and stay with it for a minute, even if it's something small.

escape.text: In 1879 the thirty-four-year-old Nietzsche gave up his professorship in Basel and never returned to a settled life. He described very precisely the urge to drop everything and leave — a job, a city, a role. In the preface to Human, All Too Human he speaks of the "great liberation" that comes to a person suddenly, like the shock of an earthquake: the desire to go away, anywhere, at any cost. Nietzsche knew it firsthand and became a wanderer, moving between the mountains and the sea. But he also honestly warned that this liberation is not the final goal, only the beginning of a long road toward "the great health"; there is much turmoil in it. This means your wish to escape may be a sign that you have outgrown your old frame. It doesn't need to be suppressed. But it's worth asking not only "what do I want to leave?" but also "who do I want to become?"
escape.practice: Say two sentences aloud: "I want to get away from…" and "I want to become…". Listen for which sounds stronger — Nietzsche would say that freedom "from" is worth something only if it leads to freedom "for."

forbidden_attraction.text: Nitimur in vetitum — "we strive for the forbidden": Nietzsche put this line from Ovid in the preface to Ecce Homo as a motto of his philosophy. Attraction to someone who is unavailable or "the wrong person" can be confusing and frightening. He meant above all forbidden thoughts, but the observation is broader: prohibition and unavailability give desire a special force. Nietzsche argued sharply against a morality that declares the passions evil and demands they be rooted out. He believed the drives are part of life; they shouldn't be hated but understood and "spiritualized", that is, turned into something meaningful. In Nietzsche's terms, your attraction is not a verdict on you. It is a force that is telling you something. You can ask: what life, what quality, what freedom do I see in this unavailable thing?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Say aloud three words for what draws you to this person or situation. Nietzsche would suggest "spiritualizing" the drive: what part of it could show up in your own life?

social_anxiety.text: Contemporaries remembered Nietzsche as shy and scrupulously polite, a man who listened more than he spoke in company. He saw the fear of others' judgment not as a personal weakness but as a common feature of human society. In his essay "Schopenhauer as Educator" he wrote that people hide behind others' opinions and customs out of timidity before the neighbour who demands they be "like everyone else". And he immediately added: every person is a unique, unrepeatable miracle, and there will never be a second such combination of traits in the world. Seen this way, your shyness is not a defect but a tension between the wish to fit in and the fact that you don't have to be a copy. Nietzsche didn't demand instant courage from you. He suggested asking yourself whose voice speaks in the fear of judgment — your own, or an internalized "neighbour's voice".
social_anxiety.practice: When the fear of being judged shows up, ask yourself: "Who exactly do I think is judging me?" Often it turns out to be the generic "neighbour" Nietzsche wrote about rather than a real person.

uncertainty.text: "To the ships, you philosophers!" Nietzsche exclaims in The Gay Science: the horizon is open again, and perhaps there has never been such an open sea. Uncertainty is hard: you long for solid ground, and there isn't any. Nietzsche knew this state and, unexpectedly, saw more than a threat in it. In The Gay Science he wrote of the free spirit who takes leave of the need for complete certainty and learns to keep its balance on the slender ropes of possibility. Elsewhere he described the feeling when the horizon is open again, like a sea on which one can set sail. In this light, uncertainty is not only anxiety but also open space: the future is not yet written, which means there is room in it for your participation. Nietzsche didn't demand that you always rejoice in the unknown. But he suggested at least sometimes noticing its other side — a freedom that doesn't exist where everything is settled.
uncertainty.practice: Look out of the window at the farthest point you can see — as at Nietzsche's open sea. Name one unknown that worries you, and one possibility that exists precisely because the outcome isn't decided yet.

waiting.text: Nietzsche waited for readers almost all his life: he had the last part of Zarathustra printed at his own expense, in about forty copies. Waiting is exhausting: an answer or some news lies somewhere ahead, and there's nothing you can do. Nietzsche offered an unusual image. In Daybreak he compared the creative person to a pregnant woman who carries within her something that grows by itself and cannot hurry its growth. This state, he wrote, calls for care and patience: we don't know exactly what is ripening, but we protect it and wait. So waiting is not empty time but a time when something is happening beyond your control. You can stop spending your strength trying to rush it. In Zarathustra the hero, too, sits and waits for his hour, surrounded by old and new tablets. Waiting without hurrying is also a skill, and it can be learned.
waiting.practice: Tell yourself, "Something is ripening, and I don't need to rush it." Then spend half an hour on something unrelated to what you're waiting for.

regret.text: To turn every "it was" into "thus I willed it" — that is how Zarathustra understands redemption from the past. Regret over what you did or didn't do has a way of coming back again and again. Nietzsche considered our relationship to the past one of the main tests. In Thus Spoke Zarathustra he describes how the will suffers because it cannot change "it was": the past is a stone it cannot move. From this, according to Nietzsche, grows "the spirit of revenge" — a grudge against time. His answer is neither to forget nor to justify yourself, but to learn to accept your past as part of the road that led you here. It follows that you can disagree with what you did and still acknowledge: this is my story, and I go on with it. Then regret stops being an accusation against yourself and becomes part of what you grow from.
regret.practice: Say aloud one sentence about something you regret, and end it with the words: "…and this, too, brought me here." Repeat the ending once more, more slowly.

quote.text: To redeem those who lived in the past and to recreate all "it was" into a "thus I willed it" — that alone should I call redemption.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

longing.text: What if the pain of absence is also a secret "yes" to what was? Nietzsche proposed a way to test it. When you miss one particular person, the feeling can be quiet and very persistent. In The Gay Science he asks: what if a demon told you that you would live this life again and again, endlessly? This is his idea of "eternal recurrence". For longing, the question is unexpectedly useful: would you want to live those moments with this person again? If so, then longing is not only the pain of absence but also proof that those moments were precious, that your life had something to say "yes" to. In other words, longing doesn't need to be driven away. It tells you that you have truly lived, and that memory remains yours.
longing.practice: Try Nietzsche's experiment: recall one moment with this person and ask yourself whether you'd want to live it again, endlessly. If so, stay in that "yes" for a minute with your eyes closed.

world_pain.text: How do you avoid drowning in others' pain without turning away from it? Nietzsche asked this more sharply than most. Wars, injustice, other people's grief in the news can weigh on you so much that it's hard to live your own life. Nietzsche is known for his critique of compassion, and it's important to understand it correctly. He didn't consider others' pain unimportant. He feared that compassion which only multiplies suffering in the world and changes nothing weakens the one who feels it, too. Instead of passive suffering-with he valued active help and shared joy — the ability to share strength and joy with others. Put simply: your sensitivity is precious, but drowning in others' pain is not the same as helping. Nietzsche would ask: what can you do, create, give? And how can you keep the strength you need in order to give, and not only to suffer?
world_pain.practice: Do one concrete thing within your power today — big or tiny. Then one thing that restores your strength: Nietzsche would say that only someone with a surplus can give.

rejection.text: Nietzsche sent his proposal to Lou Salomé through a friend — and received a polite refusal. Rejection hurts, and that pain needs no justification. That was in 1882, and soon his relationships with close friends fell apart as well. It was one of the darkest periods of his life. But almost immediately afterward he began writing Thus Spoke Zarathustra. Nietzsche believed pain should be neither denied nor endlessly chewed over; it can be "digested" and turned into something of your own — he called this sublimation, turning a strong feeling into creative force. Then a rejection is not a verdict on your worth but an event you have every right to live through and mourn. And perhaps later something will grow from it that wouldn't have existed without it.
rejection.practice: Turn some of the pain into movement, as Nietzsche turned it into work: take a walk, dance, tidy your desk. As you go, notice what desire or question this refusal has awakened in you.

abandonment.text: "O solitude, my home!" exclaims Zarathustra on returning to his cave. The fear of being abandoned can be very old and very deep. Nietzsche knew loneliness better than most: illness, broken ties, years of wandering through foreign cities. But he rethought it. In the chapter "The Homecoming" solitude speaks to Zarathustra tenderly, like a mother. This means being alone with yourself is not only a threat but also a place where you can put down roots. That doesn't mean closeness isn't needed or that the fear is wrong. But when you have a home within yourself, the fear of loss stops being a fear of vanishing. Nietzsche taught not to depend on another's presence as on air, but to be your own support — and then you are freer to love.
abandonment.practice: Spend ten minutes alone with yourself doing something pleasant — like Zarathustra in his cave. Notice what it's like to be good company for yourself.

unrequited.text: In farewell, his disciples give Zarathustra a staff with a golden handle on which a serpent coils around the sun — and he speaks to them of the "gift-giving virtue." Unrequited love is a pain in which it seems you gave something and got no answer. Nietzsche proposed a different way of looking at what it means to love. It is a love that pours out of abundance, like the sun giving its light and asking nothing in return. In Nietzsche's terms, your love is not a debt left unpaid but evidence of your own richness: your capacity to see, to admire, to wish another person well. Nietzsche wouldn't say it doesn't hurt. But he would show that this strength belongs to you and doesn't disappear because it wasn't accepted. In time it can be directed to where it will be met.
unrequited.practice: Name aloud three qualities that showed up in you in this love: generosity, attentiveness, courage — or your own. Nietzsche would say this is your wealth, and it hasn't gone anywhere.

humiliation.text: "What is the seal of attained freedom? No longer being ashamed in front of oneself" — one of the short questions and answers in Nietzsche's Gay Science. Humiliation wounds deeply because it strikes at your very dignity. Nietzsche helps you look at the scene from another side. In The Gay Science he asks a few short questions, and the answers put everything in its place. He calls bad the one who always wants to put others to shame, and most humane — sparing another from shame. Seen this way, humiliation says more about the one who humiliates than about you. Nietzsche also warned that the humiliated person risks falling into ressentiment — endlessly chewing over the hurt and building a life around it. The way out is to acknowledge the pain, not to doubt your worth, and gradually reclaim your own voice. You were made to feel shame, but shame did not become who you are.
humiliation.practice: Straighten up and walk slowly across the room, like someone who is no longer ashamed of themselves. Finish aloud: "The one who wanted to shame me showed by it…" — and "And I am still a person who…".

quote.text: Whom do you call bad? — Those who always want to put to shame. What do you consider most humane? — To spare someone shame.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

body_shame.text: Nietzsche wrote that he trusted no thought not born in the open air, while moving freely — no thought in which the muscles did not also celebrate. Dissatisfaction with your body almost always comes with other people's yardsticks. Nietzsche was one of the first philosophers to take the body's side decisively. In Thus Spoke Zarathustra there is a chapter, "On the Despisers of the Body", in which he argues with those who consider the body something lower. The body, says Zarathustra, is a "great reason", and what we call spirit is only its little tool. In this light, your body is not an object to be graded but the very life that thinks, feels and acts through you. Nietzsche didn't propose loving every feature on command. But he did suggest ceasing to see the body as an enemy and beginning to listen to it as a wise ally.
body_shame.practice: Move for a minute the way your body wants — stretch, sway, walk — without looking in the mirror. Nietzsche would call it a festival of the muscles; notice what your body is like from the inside, not the outside.

quote.text: There is more reason in your body than in your best wisdom.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
quote.source: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, "On the Despisers of the Body" (1883)

illness.text: "The great health" was conceived by a man who was almost never healthy. When your body lets you down, life narrows, and that can make you angry, frightened and worn out. Nietzsche knew this firsthand: for most of his adult life he suffered from agonizing headaches and poor eyesight, and illness forced him to leave the university. He wrote about it honestly and without embellishment. In the preface to The Gay Science he admitted he doubted that pain makes a person "better", but knew that it makes them deeper. Nietzsche spoke of "the great health" — not as the absence of illness but as the ability to live in spite of it, and even to learn from it. So you don't have to be a hero. But illness can open up a view of life that those who have always been healthy don't have.
illness.practice: Silently name one thing you've started to notice or value differently since you've been ill — a sound, a taste, someone's word. Don't judge it; just hold it in mind, like a find.

pride.text: Nietzsche gave the chapters of Ecce Homo provocative titles: "Why I Am So Wise", "Why I Am So Clever", "Why I Write Such Good Books". Pride in what you've done is a good, well-earned feeling, and he would be the last to advise you to be ashamed of it. He criticized a morality that teaches people to belittle themselves and to treat self-respect as a sin. In Beyond Good and Evil he wrote that the noble soul has reverence for itself. This is not arrogance toward others but respect for your own path and your own efforts. Nietzsche urged us to "become who you are", and pride in something you've done is one of the moments when that happens: you see that your strengths and choices have borne fruit. It follows that you can let yourself live this feeling fully, without looking over your shoulder at others' judgment.
pride.practice: Announce aloud, in Nietzsche's tone, one chapter of your own Ecce Homo: "Why I Did This Well." Finish one sentence and notice which of your strengths showed itself in it.

quote.text: The noble soul has reverence for itself.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

melancholy.text: "When I seek another word for music, I always find only the word Venice," Nietzsche confessed. Bright sadness is a state in which sorrow somehow feels good. Nietzsche knew it well. In Ecce Homo he includes his poem about Venice: at night, by a bridge, he listens to the distant song of the gondoliers, and his soul, like a stringed instrument, quietly answers it — "trembling with iridescent bliss". Sorrow and bliss don't argue here; they sound together. Nietzsche never divided life into "good" and "bad" feelings: for him the fullness of life includes both light and shadow. In other words, melancholy is not a mistake of mood but the soul's ability to resonate more finely. It doesn't need to be chased away. You can stay in it, as in evening music, and let it be part of the life to which you say "yes".
melancholy.practice: Find a few minutes today to listen to music at dusk — a Venetian barcarolle, perhaps — or simply sit in silence. Notice how sadness and tenderness sound together.
